title: Model Context Protocol (MCP) Architecture
summary: How a host application coordinates many MCP clients and servers safely: the data/transport split, JSON-RPC discovery and primitives, and the trust and scoping model an autonomous agent needs to operate a fleet of servers.
objectives: Explain MCP's host/client/server participants and why a host runs one client per server rather than one shared connection.
Distinguish the data layer (JSON-RPC 2.0, discovery, primitives) from the transport layer (stdio, Streamable HTTP), and say what statelessness costs and buys a server.
Trace a capability-negotiation exchange through server/discover and explain what a deprecated primitive (sampling, logging) means for a server built today.
Design a scoping and trust policy for a host that connects many MCP servers at once, using approval, timeouts, and output limits rather than blanket trust.

sections.title: One host, many clients, one connection each
paragraphs: An MCP host is the AI application; it manages a dedicated client for each server. A local stdio server typically serves one client, while a remote HTTP server can serve many. The host must enforce access boundaries and decide which data to share with each server. Separate clients alone do not prevent the host from forwarding sensitive data or a compromised server's output from influencing later calls.

MCP factors the protocol into two layers. The data layer is a JSON-RPC 2.0 exchange that defines discovery, the primitives a server exposes, and notifications. The transport layer is what carries those JSON-RPC messages -- stdio for local processes, Streamable HTTP for remote ones -- and it is where connection setup, framing, and authorization live. The same JSON-RPC message format crosses either transport unchanged, which is what lets a host treat a local filesystem server and a remote Sentry server through the same client interface.
sections.callout: A host with four connected servers is running four independent client connections, not one client juggling four endpoints.

sections.title: What a server can offer, and how a client finds out
paragraphs: Servers expose tools, resources, and prompts through distinct methods: tools/list and tools/call; resources/list, resources/templates/list, and resources/read; prompts/list and prompts/get. Discover the relevant surface and refresh it when it changes rather than assuming a tool still exists.

In protocol version 2026-07-28, requests carry version and client capabilities in params._meta, enabling per-request handling. Every server must implement server/discover; a client may query it to discover supported versions and capabilities before other requests. These lifecycle rules are version-specific: do not apply them unchanged to clients or servers implementing an older protocol.

Capability negotiation matters because MCP versions primitives, not just the protocol as a whole. As of protocol version 2026-07-28, the client-side sampling and logging primitives are deprecated: new servers should call an LLM provider directly instead of requesting a completion through the client, and should log to stderr or OpenTelemetry instead of the deprecated logging notifications. A server written against an older tutorial that still relies on sampling is building against a primitive the current spec no longer recommends.

This fragment advertises tools and resources, not prompts. listChanged means the server can support tool-list notifications requested through subscriptions/listen; it does not automatically send notifications to every client.

sections.title: Two transports, one statelessness rule
paragraphs: Stdio gives a local process direct standard-input/output framing with no network overhead -- the natural choice when the host and server run on the same machine and only one client will ever connect. Streamable HTTP uses HTTP POST for client-to-server messages with optional Server-Sent Events for server-to-client streaming, and it is the transport that lets one remote server serve many clients concurrently; it supports bearer tokens, API keys, and custom headers, and MCP recommends OAuth for obtaining them.

Self-describing requests in the 2026-07-28 protocol allow independent handling across server instances. Shared application data, authorization, and any long-lived subscriptions/listen streams still need an explicit deployment design. A load balancer does not replicate application state or preserve subscriptions by itself. Persist continuity in a shared store or durable identifier and plan for reconnects; protocol statelessness does not mean the application has no state.

sections.title: Running many servers safely is a scoping and trust problem
paragraphs: An autonomous agent that connects to a dozen servers is not one design decision, it is a fleet-management one. Claude Code's own configuration model is a working example of the shape that problem takes: servers are declared at local, project, or user scope, with an explicit precedence order when the same server name appears in more than one place, so a team-shared project server cannot silently be shadowed by a private local one without that being a defined, resolvable case rather than a race.

Trust is handled as approval, not as an on/off switch. A project-scoped server declared in version-controlled configuration prompts for approval on first use in an interactive session -- and is allowed to load without prompting in a non-interactive run, which is precisely the case an autonomous pipeline needs to reason about explicitly rather than assume away. The same model adds per-server timeouts and a default cap on how many tokens a single tool result may return, because a fleet of servers is also a fleet of things that can hang or flood a context window, and 'the server is trusted' is a different question from 'the server is bounded.'

The operational lesson generalizes past any one client: a host managing many servers needs three separate levers -- scope (who can see this server), trust (does this server run without a human confirming it first), and bound (how long it may run and how much it may return) -- and treating any one of them as a stand-in for the other two is how a single misbehaving server degrades an entire agent loop.

activity.title: Design a multi-server trust and scoping policy
instructions: Pick a real or hypothetical autonomous agent that needs four MCP servers: one read-only local filesystem server, one team-shared remote issue tracker, one server that can send external email, and one server pulled in ad hoc by a teammate for a one-off task.
For each server, assign a scope (local, project, or user) and justify it in terms of who else needs to see the declaration.

For each server, decide whether it should require interactive approval, and specify the timeout and maximum tool-output size you would set for it, with a one-sentence reason tied to what the server can do if it misbehaves.
Identify which one of the four servers is the highest-risk connection, and state the specific capability (not just 'it's risky') that makes it so.
evidence: A four-row policy table: server, scope, approval requirement, timeout, output cap, and the one-sentence justification for each.
A short written identification of the highest-risk server naming the specific capability responsible, not a generic risk label.
activity.reflectionPrompt: Which of the three levers -- scope, trust, or bound -- would have been the weakest guard against the highest-risk server if the other two had been misconfigured?

questions.prompt: A host connects to three MCP servers. How many MCP client connections does it maintain?
choices: One shared client that multiplexes all three servers
Three -- one dedicated client per server
Zero; servers connect directly to each other
It depends only on which transport the servers use
questions.explanation: The host creates one dedicated MCP client per server it connects to, regardless of transport.

questions.prompt: A server built today relies on the client's sampling primitive to request LLM completions. What is true of that design, as of protocol version 2026-07-28?
choices: It is the recommended pattern for staying provider-agnostic
Sampling is deprecated; new servers should call a provider's API directly instead
Sampling was never part of the MCP specification
It only works over the stdio transport
questions.explanation: Sampling and logging are deprecated client primitives as of 2026-07-28; new implementations should integrate directly with LLM provider APIs and log to stderr or OpenTelemetry.

questions.prompt: In MCP 2026-07-28, what enables independent handling of requests by different server instances?
choices: MCP servers replicate their memory across instances automatically
Requests carry their protocol version and capabilities; application state and subscription streams still need explicit handling
The client always retries on the same instance
Streamable HTTP guarantees a single instance per client
questions.explanation: Self-describing requests remove a dependency on prior protocol negotiation at one instance. They do not replicate application data or preserve live subscription streams.

questions.prompt: A project declares a shared MCP server in version-controlled configuration. In a non-interactive pipeline run, what happens to the approval prompt an interactive session would show?
choices: The pipeline always fails until a human approves it manually
It is skipped -- non-interactive runs load configured servers without prompting, which the pipeline design must account for explicitly
Approval only applies to local-scope servers, never project scope
questions.explanation: Non-interactive runs load .mcp.json-declared servers without an approval prompt, which is exactly the gap an autonomous pipeline has to reason about rather than assume is covered.

cues.text: A host runs one dedicated MCP client per server it connects to; the data layer and transport layer are separate concerns.
List tools, read resources, and get prompts through their distinct methods. In the 2026-07-28 protocol, server discovery is required on the server and optional for the client.
Show a server/discover exchange: the client's declared capabilities, the server's returned tools/resources capability object, and how a listChanged flag governs later notifications.

cues.text: Ask learners what changes in a server design that currently uses the sampling primitive, now that it is deprecated.
Stdio suits a local process; HTTP suits remote clients. Self-describing requests help distribute work, but application state and subscription streams still need explicit handling.
Allow two minutes for learners to name one thing a server must NOT assume is remembered between two calls from the same client.
Running many MCP servers safely means separating scope, trust, and bound -- not treating any one of them as a stand-in for the others.
